newsitem.title: USA: Oil imports help U.S. economy, GAO report says.
newsitem.headline: Oil imports help U.S. economy, GAO report says.

text.p: The United States reaps hundreds of billions of dollars in benefits a year from importing relatively low-cost oil instead of depending on its domestic energy sources, the General Accounting Office said on Thursday.
But the Energy Department called the analysis by Congress' investigative agency "seriously flawed," and said it yielded "no insight into the overall consequences of oil imports."
The GAO said economic benefits of oil imports outweigh infrequent price shocks that it said cost the economy an annual average in the tens of billions of dollars.

Oil accounts for about 40 percent of the nation's energy consumption, and the United States imports about half its oil, much of it from the Middle East and other politically unstable areas. Imports are projected to rise to more than 60 percent of U.S. consumption over the next 20 years.
Domestic oil producers and other critics of this situation, including the Energy Department, have said this leaves the country far too vulnerable to price shocks when import supplies are disrupted.

But the GAO disagreed, saying that unless the country reduced its overall oil use, it still would suffer price shocks even if it increased its own production since domestic prices would rise with world prices.

Lowering imports by boosting domestic production would raise employment in the oil sector, but the report said those gains would be more than offset by losses in other sectors because of higher priced oil.

Reducing oil imports by just 2 million to 3.2 million barrels per day from 2006's projected level of 11.4 million barrels per day would actually end up costing the U.S. between $50 billion and $100 billion annually in lost gross domestic product, the GAO said.

However the GAO acknowledged that dependence on imported oil "imposes military and other costs that are not easily measured" as the United States has relied on a military presence to keep oil flowing from regions such as the Gulf.

The report was prepared for House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, partly to assess the Energy Department's efforts to enhance energy security by cutting consumption and raising domestic oil output.

The Energy Department estimated that its energy efficiency programs would lead to a drop in U.S. oil use of about 2.1 million barrels per day by 2010, and that its fossil energy programs could increase U.S. oil output by 800,000 barrels per day.

But the GAO said projections show increased oil demand would offset most of those gains. Experts the GAO consulted said the United States should rely on big, quick releases of oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve to blunt price shocks.
